name: Leukocyte-rich PRP (L-PRP)

card.summary: A platelet-rich plasma preparation that keeps white blood cells in the concentrate; it is used in tendon, joint and muscle treatment and offered by some clinics for tissue repair that supports a better-looking body and recovery.
card.note: Injected procedure; preparations and results vary by clinic and system.

quick.overview:
Leukocyte-rich PRP (L-PRP) is made by centrifuging a person's own blood into a platelet concentrate that keeps white blood cells, unlike "pure" PRP which removes most of them. It is injected into injured tissue to deliver growth factors that may support healing.

Its appearance link is mostly via recovery: tendon, joint and muscle problems that limit training, or tissue repair in cosmetic work. Trials compare it with other PRP types, corticosteroid and hyaluronic acid, with mixed results across conditions.
quick.how: A clinician draws blood, spins it in a device that concentrates platelets and some leukocytes, and injects the product into the target tissue, often under ultrasound guidance. Sessions and spacing vary by condition and clinic, and it is usually described as an outpatient procedure. Results are generally described as developing over weeks.
quick.risks: Because it uses the patient's own blood, allergic reactions are uncommon, but injections can cause pain, swelling and infection risk, and leukocyte-rich products have been discussed as more inflammatory after injection. Preparation and equipment hygiene matter; products and devices differ and are regulated differently by country.

lead: Leukocyte-rich platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP) is a category of platelet concentrate defined by a high white blood cell content. A widely cited 2009 classification divides platelet concentrates by leukocyte and fibrin content into pure PRP, L-PRP, pure PRF and L-PRF, and lists commercial systems in each group.[1]

For appearance, the value people describe is recovery and repair. L-PRP is used in orthopaedic and sports medicine to treat tendons, joints and muscle, which can help someone return to training; clinics also offer PRP in cosmetic settings, where the leukocyte question applies to the product chosen.[2][3]

Research compares L-PRP with other formulations. A 2024 randomized trial reported that leukocytes did not change the safety or efficacy of PRP for knee osteoarthritis, while a 2024 review of muscle injuries said leukocyte-rich PRP appeared to have the strongest evidence in that area.[4][5]

chain: Own blood is spun into a platelet and leukocyte concentrate
Injected into injured tendon, joint or muscle
Healing may support returning to training
angle.text: L-PRP is used mainly to help injured tissue recover so people can keep training. In aesthetics, clinics may use PRP products for skin and scalp work, where the leukocyte content is one variable.

paras: Platelet concentrates differ by whether they keep leukocytes and whether they form a fibrin matrix. L-PRP contains leukocytes plus platelets and is typically liquid when injected, while L-PRF forms a fibrin clot. The classification system and its product examples are laid out in a 2009 review.[1]
A narrative review of PRP in musculoskeletal care discusses preparation, classification and mechanism, and asks which PRP type suits each indication.[6]

L-PRP has been studied for tendons, joints and muscle. A 2023 review concluded ultrasound-guided leukocyte-rich PRP injections appeared to have the strongest evidence among orthobiologics for muscle injuries, while describing clinical data as limited and inconclusive overall.[5] A small randomized trial in lateral elbow tendinopathy compared L-PRP with corticosteroid.[7]

PRP is used in skin and scalp procedures, but the studies in this area mostly concern PRP generally rather than L-PRP specifically; a review of maxillofacial applications describes the leukocyte-containing families among platelet concentrates used for tissue repair.[8]

Reviews of PRP for knee osteoarthritis have compared it with hyaluronic acid.[9] A 2022 trial reported that multiple PRP injections outperformed single injections or saline at two years.[10] A 2023 randomized trial compared pure PRP with L-PRP for knee cartilage lesions.[11] A 2024 three-arm trial examined PRP types after rotator cuff repair, noting earlier studies had not clearly shown benefit and that leukocyte concentrations had not been directly compared.[12]

Procedure-related effects include pain, swelling and infection risk at the injection site. Discussion of leukocyte content centres on whether white cells add inflammation; trials have not agreed on whether that changes results.[4][6]

Randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis, rotator cuff repair, lateral elbow pain and cartilage lesions have compared leukocyte-rich with other PRP formulations or with comparators.[4][7][10][11][12][13] Findings differ across sites: the knee osteoarthritis trial reported no effect of leukocyte content.[4] No clinical trials were found of L-PRP specifically for facial appearance.

timeline.event: Classification of platelet concentrates into P-PRP, L-PRP, P-PRF and L-PRF published.[1]
Editorial reviews L-PRP and L-PRF in medicine.[14]
